summary:
Same-sex conduct between men was decriminalised in Barbados in December 2022, following a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with the trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights programme. A High Court ruling on sodomy published in May 2023 found discrimination based on sexual orientation unconstitutional.

Enforcement against violence has produced a documented impunity outcome. In February 2018 Hoffmann was attacked with a meat cleaver by Brandon Coward and suffered serious injuries, including to her throat. Coward was convicted in April 2019 and ordered to pay Hoffmann BDS$460 (US$230) or serve three months in prison; no jail time was imposed.

Employment protection does not reach gender identity or gender expression. Trans Barbadians are frequently fired or denied jobs for dressing wrong, and the Employment (Prevention of Discrimination) Act, 2020, passed by Parliament in August 2020, bars discrimination on grounds including sex, sexual orientation and domestic partnership status but is read by Hoffmann as excluding trans workers because neither gender identity nor gender expression is listed.

Barbados law recognises no union between two people of the same sex. In June 2016 the government ruled out changing the law to allow same-sex marriage, and in September 2020 it announced only a plan to recognise some form of civil union followed by a referendum on gay marriage. Critics called the civil union proposal unnecessarily vague and expected the referendum to fail; as of the source's account neither had been enacted.

Entry and migration policy treats LGBT people as a contested category rather than a protected one. Barbados does not screen or protect LGBT travellers as a distinct group, and the government has questioned the legitimacy of LGBT migration: in 2011 it said it was investigating claims that gay Barbadians were seeking refugee status in Canada, and in 2016 Foreign Minister Maxine McClean described such applications as an attempt to abuse the Canadian refugee system, noting that two of nine Canadian applications had been denied.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa, introduced in July 2020, initially allowed foreign workers to bring only an opposite-sex spouse; it was changed to permit same-sex spouses.

Family recognition is closed to same-sex couples. They cannot legally adopt, surrogacy is illegal although not explicitly prohibited or regulated by law, and same-sex couples are not recognised as families. The Barbados Fertility Centre offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.

Official and religious hostility is on the record. In 2016 Attorney General Adriel Brathwaite said Barbados would not change the law to allow same-sex marriage, and after David Cameron's 2011 CHOGM aid warning over sodomy laws he said Barbados would not be dictated to by the United Kingdom. A government minister warned that external forces were trying to impose same-sex marriage, prompting Human Rights Watch to call the response a cheap political trick, since its report did not mention same-sex marriage. Fundamentalist groups including the New Testament Church have claimed sexual orientation is chosen and argued that discrimination against LGBT people should be encouraged, and human rights activists say the arrival of more American evangelical ministers has spread homophobic rhetoric more widely. The Barbados Nation's informal comment line drew opposition to a proposed gay tourism package. The Anglican Bishop of Barbados and the Catholic Church oppose the buggery law while stating respect for LGBT rights, and Prime Minister Mia Mottley, elected in May 2018, is reportedly pro-LGBT.

A regional human-rights route remains open. In 2018 activists filed a case with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights challenging the Sexual Offences Act (Ch.154, ss.9 and 12); the Commission gave the government three months to respond in late July 2019, and failure to repeal could send the matter to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights for a binding decision.
tangentialFactors:
The Human Dignity Trust treats the Barbados litigation as one of several constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes in the Eastern Caribbean, so the December 2022 outcome is a regional data point as much as a national one.

Under the former Section 12 of the Sexual Offences Act, serious indecency carried a maximum penalty of ten years in prison where the act was committed on or towards a person aged 16 or older. The same statute, at sections 9 and 12, is the one now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.
localsOnly:
Barbados Gays, Lesbians and All-Sexuals Against Discrimination (BGLAD) was founded in 2013 by Donnya Piggott and Ro-Ann Mohammed to create an education mechanism and open public dialogue for the LGBT community. Pride events have served an awareness-raising function: a first small event in November 2017 and a parade of about 120 people on Rihanna Drive, Bridgetown, in July 2018. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in November 2018 with the local organisation NOW and veteran trans advocates, and Hoffmann has given a first-person account of visibility and danger on the island.

Residents have sought protection abroad in numbers the government disputes. A 2016 Guyanese newspaper reported that over 300 LGBT people in Barbados were seeking asylum in Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States, and UGLAAB said it would investigate the same allegations.

Relationship and family law leaves same-sex couples without recognition: no union is recognised, adoption is unavailable to same-sex couples, and surrogacy is illegal though not explicitly prohibited or regulated. The Barbados Fertility Centre offers IVF and artificial insemination to lesbian couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
No sourced findings were identified on legal gender recognition or identity-document processes for trans people in Barbados.

No findings were identified on trans-specific custody, parental rights or family law outcomes.

No findings were identified on access to transition-related healthcare, mental health or specialist care. The only health-related provisions in the source inventory are the Barbados Fertility Centre's IVF and artificial insemination for lesbian couples, the illegal status of surrogacy, and UGLAAB's AIDS work.

No findings were identified on the treatment of LGBT minors, the detention of unaccompanied youth, or school-based anti-bullying and gender-affirming education.
